Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina. An Italian Renaissance composer who lived around 1525 to 1594 and became revered for his crystalline polyphonic masses and motets. His music epitomized what became known as the stile palestriniano: a modal, thoroughly singable sacred idiom that emphasized clarity and spiritual restraint.

Palestrina composed over one hundred masses. Many employed the parody technique, which means he would rework earlier secular songs into sacred forms. His Missa Papae Marcelli became especially celebrated for the clarity of its Latin text, allowing listeners to hear the words even within complex polyphony. He served as maestro di cappella of the Julian Chapel, which was the papal choir in Rome, a position of immense prestige and influence. He was a master of the prima prattica, the strict counterpoint rules of the Renaissance. This meant prioritizing harmonic perfection and strict voice-leading over dramatic expression, a deliberate choice that shaped everything he wrote.

His motet repertoire includes over two hundred fifty works, many set to liturgical texts and characterized by modal harmony and seamless vocal lines. A story long held that his Missa Papae Marcelli actually saved polyphonic music from a church ban during the Counter-Reformation by demonstrating that complex counterpoint could preserve text intelligibility. He established the template for a cappella sacred music: unaccompanied voices in balanced harmony, no instrumental doubling, and a deeply spiritual restraint that influenced church music composition for centuries.
